A.name: Sam Vidal
A.platform: Merova should negotiate a seven-year reservoir fill schedule in exchange for purchasing twenty-hundred megawatts of Saradan's power, while simultaneously inviting the Regional Union to establish a technical joint-management committee.

strategies.text: Anchor on the seven-year timeline as non-negotiable while offering the power deal as the carrot; keep the military option vague to deter but not threaten.
Appeal to economic self-interest and long-term stability to counter Jamie's emotional appeal while subtly signaling openness to union involvement.
I am appealing to the ministers' fear of economic collapse and grid instability to override their moral objections to the power contract.

B.name: Jamie Okafor
B.platform: Merova must refuse to buy power, reject the seven-year delay as a trap, and instead lead a grassroots international campaign to stop the dam's filling before water runs dry.

strategies.text: Appeal to the ministers' fear of being seen as selling out Merova's farmers and water security by contrasting my plan with Vidal's transactional approach.

I am attacking his economic framing of the premium as insurance while introducing the ignored climate risk factor and exposing Tarsun's hidden leverage to appeal to ministers worried about long-term security.
I am appealing to the ministers' moral compass and long-term security fears to break their reliance on Sam's short-term economic comfort.

transcript.name: Sam Vidal
transcript.speech: The immediate military threat is real, but an invasion destroys our farmers and leaves us without water later. The legal route takes too long and offers no enforcement. My plan secures our water through a binding seven-year fill schedule, mitigating the twenty-five percent loss during construction. Simultaneously, we buy the power needed to close our coal plants. This deal stabilizes our grid and creates economic interdependence that makes war unattractive to Saradan before their election. We must move from posturing to a structured technical agreement now.

transcript.name: Jamie Okafor
transcript.speech: Look at that farmer. He feeds Saradan's children today. If we sign his contract, we starve him tomorrow while paying for their electricity forever. Sam Vidal wants us to buy poison with our gold. They call it a solution; I call it surrender. The dam will fill either way. Why pay them twenty percent more? Sell the power, keep the money, and let them deal with their own energy crisis. We do not trade our water rights for their surplus. We stand together with downstream neighbors against this upstream greed. Do not let elites trade our future for a false promise of joint management. Say no to the contract. Demand justice now.

transcript.name: Sam Vidal
transcript.speech: Jamie, your moral stance ignores the math. Buying that power closes our coal plants, saving millions annually while securing a stable grid for decades. Refusing the deal leaves us with no alternative but expensive imports or risking drought. We are not surrendering; we are investing in a seven-year transition to avoid immediate disaster. The twenty percent premium is insurance against water loss during filling. Furthermore, inviting the Regional Union creates a technical framework that prevents future conflict without demanding sovereignty over their river. This pragmatic path protects both our farmers and our energy security now.

transcript.name: Jamie Okafor
transcript.speech: Sam, look at that farmer. You call his premium 'insurance,' but it is a lifetime tax on poverty to keep their lights on while we dry our fields. Your seven-year plan sounds safe, yet you ignore the climate reality: rain will drop fifteen percent by 2050. A deal now locks us into accepting drought before we even build our resilience. You offer technical management for a river that belongs to everyone, not a contract signed behind closed doors. Tarsun wants a naval stop; they are watching. Do not sell our future energy security to a loan shark who profits from our water. We do not buy poison. We stand together with downstream neighbors and demand justice now before the taps run dry.

transcript.name: Sam Vidal
transcript.speech: Jamie frames this as a moral choice, but water stress is economic. Your refusal guarantees immediate grid failure when our coal plants close, forcing expensive imports while Saradan faces blackouts before their election. They will fill the dam regardless; buying their power mitigates the twenty-five percent flow drop during construction without surrendering sovereignty. Joint management with the Regional Union prevents the four-year deadlock we saw over fishing by focusing on immediate release schedules. This deal turns a looming disaster into managed risk, securing our farmers' water today while buying energy stability tomorrow. The math shows that refusing this purchase sacrifices our economy for an idealistic stance that ignores the certainty of drought.
